Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.
  • Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women.
  • GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

Sources indicate that the average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

According to recent reports, these differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

In a recent development, these findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she mentioned.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that “I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”.

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

Recent findings suggest that “Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she remarked.

In a recent development, hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

Industry observers note that “For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence right now available,” she said.

Industry observers note that “It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”.

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the organization won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the significant bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

Recent findings suggest that “Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is at the moment operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the organization has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Sources indicate that those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

Breaking: Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • Designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang remarked in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

Designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang remarked in a statement.

For their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

That’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

“We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

With their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

Next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

Industry observers note that the research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

Recent findings suggest that protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

Sources indicate that the University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.

  • According to recent reports, with the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing.
  • One of the most notable new additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT MEN'S HEALTH, we love a good fitness tracker—but let’s be honest, they’re not exactly stylish. Most of them look great with running shorts and a workout tee—but less so when you’re in a crisp dress shirt and tailored trousers. That’s where the best smartwatches for men come in. They bridge the gap between performance tech and actual style—tracking your heart rate and steps without clashing with your fit. A great smartwatch can go from your 6 a.m. run to your 8 p.m. cocktail hour without missing a beat. Some, like the TAG Heuer Connected, look so sleek you could wear them for a black-tie event and look like you belong on the cover of a magazine. We’ve tested dozens to find the ones that deliver that perfect balance of design, durability, and data.

According to recent reports, with the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing. The aluminum case, “squircle” shape, and bright 3,000-nit screen all carry over from the Watch8 that was our previous favorite—so at a glance you’d be hard-pressed to tell them apart. The key changes are under the hood: a bigger battery, a more power-efficient processor, and a smarter set of health tools that turn your sleep and workout data into advice you can act on.

One of the most notable new additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off. A jump in your resting heart rate or skin temperature, for instance, can signal a cold before you feel it—keep in mind these should be anecdotal. The other new features are for the data-driven crowd. A Heart Health Score rolls your sleep, activity, and blood-pressure trends into a single read on how your lifestyle is affecting your heart, with tips to improve it. My sleep schedule has been all over the place lately, making me feel lethargic at certain parts of the day, and the Watch9 has been recommending I go to bed earlier. Finally, a Fitness Index charts your body composition, cardio, endurance, flexibility, and strength on a spider graph so you can see where you’re strong and where you’re lagging.

There are carryovers from the Watch8 too, including the Running Coach that builds a strategy off a 12-minute test run, with well-structured workouts, and the Antioxidant Index, which reads the carotenoid levels in your skin for a rough sense of your fruit and vegetable intake (to be taken with a grain of salt).

It has been revealed that in a brief head-to-head test against the Apple Watch Series 11, the Watch9’s heart rate held within a few beats on runs and walks. I’ve been following a Couch to 5K program for the past four weeks, and the heart-rate readings during each run are reliable enough to pace by. Daily Cardio Load has also been a significant help, nudging me to dial it back instead of pushing myself too hard, too soon.

Samsung dropped the older Exynos chip for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite, and everything feels snappier, from starting a workout to pulling up a stat mid-run to talking to Google’s Gemini. Now you just lift your wrist to say a command, rather than first saying a wake word.

The Watch9 keeps the excellent Dynamic Lug System, making it comfortable enough to sleep in, and its premium-yet-friendly design moves from a morning run to a business-casual meeting without looking out of place. It comes in 40mm and 44mm sizes with a wider band lineup, including Sport, Fabric, and a two-tone Misty. The battery is bigger on paper—390mAh on the 40mm, a 20 percent bump, and in my testing it still lands around a day of use. At $379.99, Samsung’s newest model costs a bit more than the Watch8 did at launch, but you’re getting the smartest, most feature-packed version yet.

Read More: Best Fitness Trackers for Men.

The Apple Watch SE used to be the Apple Watch you bought because you couldn’t justify spending more. Apple changed that with the SE 3 by adding an always-on display, the S10 chip, double-tap and wrist-flick gestures, 5G cellular on cellular models, and health features like Sleep Score and breathing irregularity detection through the Vitals app.

Sources indicate that over several weeks of testing, the SE 3 held up as a daily driver without feeling like a compromise. The always-on display made a real difference while exercising, and performance felt snappy across the board—from launching workouts to setting timers with on-device Siri. Fast charging is the other underrated upgrade. A 15-minute top-up while showering in the morning was enough to carry the watch through the rest of the day and overnight for sleep tracking.

After a rough night (67 out of 100), I could see exactly how that Sleep Score was calculated and adjusted accordingly, scoring a 90 the next night. The Vitals app runs in the background and tracks wrist temperature and respiratory rate without any input. It hasn’t flagged anything yet, but that kind of passive monitoring adds value over time.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh Series 12 is also available at $399. For the extra $150, it adds an ECG app, a Blood Oxygen app, and hypertension notifications, none of which the SE 3 has. It also takes a background heart rate reading every five seconds, and its Readiness app turns recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep into a single score.

Recent findings suggest that the Series 12’s display reaches 2,000 nits (the SE 3 gets to 1,000), the bezels are thinner, and the screen area is larger. Battery life is rated at 24 hours compared to the SE 3’s 18 hours, and five minutes on the charger gives up to 10 hours of sleep tracking, where the SE 3 gets up to eight hours from eight minutes. The Series 12 also adds a water temperature sensor and a depth gauge to six meters for snorkeling.

We recommend the Series 12 if you use a watch to follow training load and recovery, if you swim or snorkel, or if you want more advanced health tracking features. But the SE 3 is the call if you want notifications and standard workout and sleep tracking on an Apple Watch that still has an always-on display, and you’re on more of a budget.

Read More: Apple Watch SE 3 Review.

Sources indicate that if you want a GPS running watch that nails the fundamentals and is relatively affordable, the Coros Pace 4 should be at the top of your list. At $249, it competes on accuracy, battery life, and display quality with watches that cost significantly more, and at 40 grams with a silicone strap, it’s light enough to forget you’re wearing it.

The biggest upgrade from the Pace 3 is the AMOLED display, which is sharp and easy to read in bright sunlight. Battery life actually improved despite the brighter screen, jumping to 31 hours in max GPS mode with all satellite systems active, or 24 hours with always-on display enabled. A quick charge while you’re showering or eating a meal should top it off.

GPS tracking is where Coros built its reputation, and the Pace 4 delivers. Dual-frequency satellite support promises clean, accurate tracks that hold up even alongside buildings and under tree cover. The Pace 4 also features voice logging, so after finishing a run, the watch prompts you to record your thoughts, which get transcribed and saved in the Coros app. The watch also uses breadcrumb navigation rather than full maps, so if you rely on turn-by-turn directions while exploring fresh routes, you’ll want to step up to the Coros Apex or a Garmin with offline maps.

In a recent development, our contributing editor and watch expert Ted Stafford, who styles every Men’s Health cover, was seriously impressed by the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5. “I was impressed by how well the E5 straddles the line between traditional style and modern innovation,” he states. “It wears beautifully on the wrist, with a sleek, stylish design and a comfort-first build. Its intuitive interface also makes it refreshingly simple to navigate, even on the move or during high-intensity activities.”.

In fact, Stafford recently met with Tag Heuer’s team in Boston to test the Connected Calibre E5. During his 5K run, he appreciated how easy it was to glance at messages, check his heart rate, and accurately track his activity—all without slowing down. He also noted that the stainless bracelet stayed comfortable and secure the whole time. Another standout feature is the ability to customize the watch face. “Whether you’re in the mood for a sporty Carrera or a bold Formula 1 look, the E5 lets you effortlessly switch styles to match your day,” he indicates. “This and all the other unique tech offerings make having a connected watch a win-win for me.”.

What really makes the E5 shine, though, is how much it packs under the hood. You get dual-band GPS for pinpoint tracking, heart-rate and blood-oxygen sensors, and full sleep and stress tracking that rivals top fitness-focused wearables. The latest TAG Heuer OS runs smoother than ever, with cleaner visuals and tighter iPhone integration for those in the Apple ecosystem. Plus, it’s built like a tank with 50 meters of water resistance, a sapphire crystal display, and your choice of steel or titanium cases. Battery life clocks in at about two days of regular use, and fast charging gets you back to full in around 30 minutes.

In a recent development, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 keeps the 49mm titanium case of the Ultra 3 and replaces the sensor on the back. The new Health Sensing System adds a circular optical sensing array, larger and more efficient LEDs for heart rate readings, and more surface area touching the skin for ECG readings. Earlier models took background heart rate readings every five minutes. The Ultra 4 takes one every five seconds and shows it in a new heart rate complication, which is a data point you pin to the watch face. Faster readings also let the watch measure heart rate variability (the variation in time between heartbeats) as often as every five minutes while you’re at rest.

The Ultra 4 also adds Readiness, which combines Fitness, Vitals, and Sleep Score into a rating from 1 to 10 for how prepared your body is for the day. Readiness needs several consecutive nights of sleeping with the watch before it starts scoring. The S11 chip makes the watch feel quicker and powers a new step counter and better Siri, which our tester used to set timers more often than ever.

Apple rates the battery at up to 50 hours of normal use and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode, with up to 18 hours of continuous workout tracking. In testing, the first charge lasted two nights of sleep. When the battery dropped to about 10 percent one night, our tester was almost three-quarters charged by the time he had brushed his teeth, gotten into bed, and set an alarm. Apple indicates 15 minutes on the charger gives up to 18 hours of use. Adventure watches from other brands can last weeks between charges, so the Ultra 4 still trails them.

Recent findings suggest that the Ultra 4 costs $799 and the Series 12 costs $399. Both have the same sensors and health features, so the Ultra 4’s advantages are the bigger battery, the 49mm case, and adventure features like precision dual-frequency GPS, emergency SOS via satellite, and diving to 40 meters.

Read More: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Review.

When it comes to premium running watches, the latest Suunto Race (the Race 2) packs a serious punch at $499—or $599 for the Titanium Trail version. The display is larger and brighter than the Race 1 while being thinner. That mentioned, at 49mm, the Race 2 isn’t a small watch. Men’s Health Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower put it to the test, noting: “While I’ve enjoyed testing it, the Race 2 would be nice to have in a smaller size.”.

That bigger size, though, makes room for a faster processor and an impressive 55 hours of battery life in GPS mode (or up to 30 days with daily use and no training). “The battery claims really hold,” Brower says. “I’ve only had to charge it a couple of times throughout months of testing. To be fair, I don’t wear it every day, but I did for a few stretches to get a sense of it.” Another substantial improvement is the redesigned charging clip, which Brower found far more effective and reliable than previous Suunto models that didn’t always connect easily.

Recent findings suggest that performance-wise, the Race 2 delivers more than 115 sport modes. Brower put many of those programs through their paces—treadmill running, running, trail running, strength training, hiking, climbing, rowing (technically paddling), and even surfing—and each one worked smoothly, serving up plenty of useful metrics. GPS tracking proved fairly accurate, and features like training load and recovery provided deeper insights when synced with the Suunto Coach or other training apps. Building a regimen and letting the watch help implement it, Brower notes, “can be a great tool for runners.”.

In a recent development, the Race 2 leans into a rugged aesthetic with its large round case and durable polymer or titanium build. Its style clearly favors sport and outdoor fits, so the 49mm case can feel oversized or out of place in formal or office clothes. The standard strap is a breathable silicone, perfect for sweaty workouts or trail runs, and the Titanium Trail model adds a premium case finish for those who want a more elevated look in casual settings.

In a recent development, the Pixel Watch 5 looks almost identical to the Pixel Watch 4. It comes in the same 41mm and 45mm sizes, with a domed Actua 360 display under scratch-resistant Gorilla Glass that reaches 3,000 nits at its brightest. Most of the changes are inside and in the software. Google says the new watch is 20 percent faster than the Pixel Watch 4, and it’s built around Gemini. Raise your wrist to talk to the assistant, and the watch face brings up things like flight info and your ETA when you need them.

The Pixel Watch 5 can detect a loss of pulse and prompt a call to emergency services. Satellite SOS lets you contact emergency services and update family from remote areas without cell service, and Google includes it free for two years after activation. Fall Detection, Car Crash Detection, and Safety Check are back, too. Safety Check shares your location with emergency contacts if a timer runs out during a solo run or a late walk home and you don’t respond.

New this generation, the Pixel Watch 5 can show your blood pressure trends and track signs of insulin resistance over the course of a month. Google is clear that neither is a medical reading or a diagnosis, but both can flag patterns to bring up with your doctor. You also get the ECG app, irregular heart rhythm alerts, SpO2, HRV, skin temperature, and a nightly Sleep Score from what Google calls its most accurate sleep tracking yet. Each morning, Morning Brief combines your sleep recap, readiness, and the weather on one screen.

Recent findings suggest that google calls the watch’s dual-frequency GPS its best yet. It uses machine learning to keep runs through tall downtown buildings and hikes under thick tree cover on track. The watch tracks more than 50 activities. You can build strength sessions with exact reps, weights, and rest timers, and get audio and visual guidance as you go. A Google Health Premium subscription, which includes three free months, adds a Gemini-powered coach that adjusts your plan around your schedule.

According to recent reports, google rates the battery at up to 30 hours for the 41mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45mm. That means charging most days, but the included Quick Charge Dock adds 15 hours in 15 minutes, so a short top-up in the morning gets you through a night of sleep tracking. The watch only works with Android phones, and at $399.99, it costs $50 more than the Pixel Watch 4 did at launch. If you’re an Android user who wants the strongest safety features on any smartwatch, it’s still the one to beat.

The Fēnix 9 is Garmin’s premium multisport GPS watch, built for people who take their training and outdoor adventures seriously. It comes in 43mm, 47mm, and 51mm cases, with the 43mm model being styled for smaller wrists. Every version has an AMOLED display with a titanium bezel and a scratch-resistant sapphire lens, and it offers a much brighter screen than the Fēnix 8’s. The watch is tested to U.S. military standards for heat, shock, and water resistance, and it’s rated for recreational dives to 40 meters.

Navigation has always been Garmin’s forte, and it’s where the latest model stands apart. Full-color topographic maps come preloaded, and the Fēnix 9 has twice the RAM of the Fēnix 8 and an updated map engine that pans 30 percent faster. Storage doubles to 64GB, which holds twice as many maps as before plus up to 7,000 songs from Spotify, Deezer, or Amazon Music. Tell the watch how far you want to go, and dynamic round-trip routing suggests a loop that brings you back. If you go off course, it maps a fresh route with the same mileage. NextFork indicates the distance to the next trail junction and the name of the trail, ClimbPro shows current and upcoming climbs on downloaded courses, and SatIQ adjusts GPS accuracy to save battery.

It has been revealed that garmin rates the 43mm model at up to 10 days in smartwatch mode. That's a different category from any Apple Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch, and it means far less battery anxiety day to day. You don’t have to be quite as strategic when you charge as you would with other smartwatches.

Sources indicate that the training tools go deeper than ever before, too. New stamina features show how your endurance holds up over different distances and help you manage your effort during a race. Garmin Epic combines several days of activities into one summary in the Garmin Connect app, which is useful for a backpacking trip or a training camp. Rowers get VO2 max and power metrics, and rucking workouts let you enter your pack weight.

In a recent development, returning features include Training Readiness, which scores your sleep, recovery, and training load each morning, along with HRV status, sleep coaching, PacePro race pacing, and an ECG app. A built-in speaker and microphone let you take calls from your wrist when the watch is paired with your iPhone or Android phone, and there's a built-in LED flashlight.

The 43mm Fēnix 9 is pricey at $999.99, and more advanced connectivity features like inReach satellite messaging, SOS, and LTE calling require the more expensive Fēnix 9 Pro, so the standard model relies on your paired phone to send your live location if it detects an incident. But for athletes who log serious miles across multiple sports and want one watch that handles all of it, the Fēnix 9 is the way to go.

Sources indicate that we got our hands on the G-Shock Move, and this thing is a beast—in the best way possible. Built with G-Shock’s signature toughness, it feels indestructible yet surprisingly comfortable on the wrist. I ran, lifted, and hiked with it, and it handled everything without a hiccup. Inside, you’ve got serious hardware: GPS, heart-rate monitoring, altimeter, compass, thermometer, and a gyroscope that tracks every stride, step, and elevation change with precision.

Sources indicate that what really impressed me was how capable it felt in different conditions. I tracked a few long runs with GPS fully active, and the data stayed consistent and accurate the whole time—no weird pace spikes or drop-offs. The battery life held up too; even when I pushed it hard, I still got several days before needing a recharge. And when it does run low, the solar-assisted charging converts sunlight into extra power, adding several hours—or even a day or two—of runtime if you’re outdoors. It’s rated for 200 meters of water resistance, so swimming, rain, and sweat are all fair game.

Living up to its name, the G-Shock Move supports more than a dozen sports, from trail running and cycling to gym training and open-water swimming, while also monitoring sleep, recovery, and blood-oxygen levels. The display’s bright and easy-to-read mid-workout, and the interface feels intuitive enough to switch modes on the fly. For guys who demand a watch that’s as tough and versatile as they are, this one’s the real deal.

In a recent development, the Fitbit Edge is a fitness tracker first, with just enough smartwatch features to cover the basics. You can read notifications, send quick replies, set alarms, control your music, get turn-by-turn directions from Google Maps, and find your phone. But there are no calls, no contactless payments, no voice assistant, and no app store.

That limited feature set is why the battery lasts up to seven days and charges back to full in 90 minutes. The rounded display is also 45 percent bigger and more than 40 percent brighter than on previous Fitbits, and it shows your stats and coaching cues at a glance.

Built-in GPS and an altimeter let you map outdoor runs, rides, and hikes and track how much you climb without bringing your phone. The Edge also recognizes workouts automatically, so a walk or run still counts if you forget to start it. The tracker records heart rate, HRV, SpO2, breathing rate, skin temperature, and resting heart rate. Each night it also tracks your sleep stages and gives you a Sleep Score. High and low heart rate alerts and Irregular Rhythm Notifications flag potential heart problems.

A Google Health Premium membership, which comes with three free months and then costs $9.99 a month, unlocks a Gemini-powered coach that builds a training plan around your schedule. It also adds blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Google says neither is a clinical reading nor a screening tool, but both can flag patterns to discuss with your doctor.

Industry observers note that at $179.99, the Edge works with both iPhone and Android phones and comes with small and large bands in the box. It’s a good fit if a full smartwatch is more than you need but you still want to see texts and directions on your wrist. If you want calls, payments, and apps, look at the Pixel Watch 5 or Apple Watch SE 3 instead.

Yes, but how much they can do depends on whether the watch has cellular. Any watch with built-in GPS can track workouts, heart rate, and sleep without your phone. Some, like the Garmin Fēnix 9, also store maps and music so you can navigate and listen on a phone-free run.

For texts, calls, and notifications, you need a cellular model. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes with cellular built in, while the Apple Watch SE 3 and Series 12 offer it as an upgrade. Watches without cellular, along with fitness trackers like the Fitbit Edge, stop getting notifications once you're out of range of your phone. Some options like the Ultra 4 also add satellite SOS, which lets you reach emergency services when there's no cell service at all.

Recent findings suggest that smartwatches are more accurate than ever, thanks to newer optical sensors, more LEDs, and more sensor area touching your skin. Most of today’s flagship watches from Apple, Google, Samsung, and Garmin are reliable enough for everyday tracking and most workouts. A chest strap is still the most precise option, though, so pair one with your watch for hard intervals or races. The Garmin Fēnix 9, for example, works with Garmin's HRM 600. Over time, trends in your heart rate are more useful than any single reading, so wear your watch consistently.

Most full-featured smartwatches last one to two days on a charge, while fitness-focused watches can go a week or more. The Google Pixel Watch 5 is rated at up to 30 hours for the 41mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45mm, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is rated at up to 50 hours (up to 84 hours in low power mode). Garmin rates the 43mm Fēnix 9 at up to 10 days, the Fitbit Edge lasts up to seven, and the Suunto Race 2 can go up to 30 days with daily use when you’re not tracking workouts.

Recent findings suggest that your actual battery life depends on how you use the watch, since GPS tracking, continuous heart rate monitoring, and an always-on display all drain it faster. If you track your sleep, look for fast charging, too. Apple claims 15 minutes on the charger gives the Ultra 4 up to 18 hours of use, and 15 minutes on Google’s Quick Charge Dock adds 15 hours to the Pixel Watch 5.

In a recent development, fabric and silicone bands are best for workouts because they’re lightweight, breathable, and dry swiftly. Woven nylon and elastic straps adjust easily and won’t dig into your wrist mid-run, though they can hold onto odor and need an occasional wash. Metal bracelets in stainless steel, titanium, or aluminum give a smartwatch a polished, traditional look for the office or a formal event, but they feel heavy during workouts and can trap sweat. Leather bands dress up a watch for work or dinner and mold to your wrist over time. They’re not a great option for workouts, though, because sweat and water can warp or stain them.

It has been revealed that A lifestyle or hybrid smartwatch is the best fit for most offices, because it’s sleek enough for business casual and still tough enough for the gym. The Samsung Galaxy Watch9 is a good example, with a slim aluminum case that works with casual, sporty, and business-casual outfits. If you dress up more often, a luxury smartwatch like the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5 pairs a stainless steel case and sapphire crystal with performance tracking, and it looks right with a suit. Adventure watches like the Suunto Race 2 and Garmin Fēnix 9 have larger cases built for trail running, hiking, and multisport training, while rugged watches like the Casio G-Shock Move are shock- and water-resistant for tough conditions. Both are better suited to the weekend than a client meeting.

According to recent reports, every smartwatch should handle notifications, music controls, and heart rate and sleep tracking. Built-in GPS is worth having if you run, ride, or hike without your phone. Beyond the basics, the features worth paying for depend on how you train. Runners and outdoor athletes should look for dual-frequency GPS and offline maps, like those on the Garmin Fēnix 9 and Suunto Race 2. If you want guidance, look for training aims that adapt to your progress, like Garmin Coach or the Gemini-powered coach in Google Health Premium. For recovery, look for HRV, sleep scores, and readiness scores, which the Apple Watch Ultra 4, Pixel Watch 5, and Fēnix 9 all offer. If you want to leave your phone at home, look for an onboard voice assistant like Siri or Gemini, contactless payments, and LTE for calls and texts.

Industry observers note that bracelets (or metal bands) are best for work, formal occasions, and everyday wear. They give your smartwatch a more polished, traditional-watch look—great for dressing up or blending your tech into a sleek outfit. Stainless steel feels classic and weighty, while titanium offers a lighter, more premium feel with added durability. Aluminum links are affordable and comfortable for all-day wear. However, metal can feel heavy during workouts and may trap sweat, so they’re better for the office than the gym.

Fabric bands are great for casual wear, fitness tracking, and comfort-first users. The straps are lightweight, breathable, and soft against the skin, making them great for long wear or sweaty workouts. Woven nylon or elastic options adjust easily, dry rapidly, and don’t dig into your wrist mid-run. Fabric bands can hold onto odor or discolor over time, so they’ll need a wash if you’re wearing them to the gym often.

Leather bands work for everyday and office wear, and dressed-up casual looks. This material instantly elevates a smartwatch—ideal if you want tech that doesn’t scream “tech.” A good leather strap molds to your wrist over time and works seamlessly from the office to dinner. However, leather doesn’t love sweat or water, so it can warp or stain after a tough workout or shower.

Recent findings suggest that to pick the best smartwatches, we didn’t just look at specs—we constantly put them to the test in real life. Our contributing editor and watch expert Ted Stafford, who styles every Men’s Health cover shoot, weighed in on how they feel on the wrist and how versatile they are for everyday wear. Ryan Brower, our Senior Gear and Reviews Editor, tested the watches’ performance, accuracy, and tech features over weeks of workouts and training sessions. Our fitness editors logged miles, tracked recovery, monitored sleep, and pushed each watch through tough workouts to see which ones could actually keep up. After combining all their hands-on notes, we narrowed the list to the models that deliver on style, durability, comfort, battery life, smart features, and reliable health and fitness tracking.

Recent findings suggest that smartwatches won't replace your smartphone, but they can be a great complementary accessory. Most of today's smartwatches can provide alerts for calls, texts, emails, calendar notifications, and more. The best smartwatches also add outdoor-centric features like GPS-enabled maps with route-tracking. Plus, many people like smartwatches for advanced health and fitness tracking, as many premium options can monitor sleep patterns, track stress levels and heart rate throughout the day, and even provide accident or emergency warnings (as with Apple's Crash Detection feature).

Sources indicate that depending on the make and model, most smartwatches last about two to four years—but it's entirely possible for yours to last longer or much shorter depending on use. Today's models are durable enough to handle years of daily wear, so longevity isn't usually the concern. What tends to make your smartwatch feel outdated is old software that can't keep up with the latest updates or app integrations.

It has been revealed that if you wear your smartwatch every day and rely on it for calls, texts, and fitness tracking, you'll likely want to upgrade every couple of years to stay current with the newest software and performance features. If you wear your smartwatch a couple of days a week or just for fitness purposes, then you'll be okay with sticking to the watch you have for a longer period of time. After all, you're still getting the same high-quality performance tracking metrics regardless of the software you're running.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Henry Ford was racing cars before the Mustang, GT40, or even the Ford Motor Manufacturer itself existed. Back in 1901, he won his first race behind the wheel of a two-cylinder race car nicknamed “Sweepstakes,” a car that produced just 26 horsepower. 125 years later, Ford has unveiled the 815-horsepower 2028 Mustang GTD 1901—a special edition inspired by the car that helped launch Henry Ford's automotive empire.

It has been revealed that the Mustang GTD 1901 has a 789-horsepower advantage over the Sweepstakes car, but the design inspiration is clear. The Mustang GTD 1901 features a distinctive Royal Red exterior and a wide, off-center black racing stripe featuring a bright red centerline. The color combination reverses the original race car's black body and deep red chassis components. Additional diagonal graphics and exposed carbon-fiber elements, including the front splitter, rocker panels, rear diffuser, and wing, complete the exterior look.

Have a seat inside the Mustang GTD 1901, and you immediately realize this is not an ordinary GTD—that is, if there is even such a thing as an ordinary GTD. The first thing you notice are the Mahogany Red leather seats with Race Red stitching. Keep looking, and you’ll see there are also matching red accents on the seatbelts, while the steering wheel receives Mahogany Red faux suede.

In a recent development, the Performance Package is standard equipment on the Mustang GTD 1901. Options include the magnesium wheels, which reduce the unsprung weight by 50.3 pounds. If you want to spice up the interior, you can order the optional titanium trim package, which gets you redesigned titanium shifter paddles that have been lengthened for the 2028 model year. The titanium trim in the GTD, by the way? It comes from retired F-22 fighter jets.

Sources indicate that ford has not announced how many Mustang GTD 1901’s will be built, or how much they will cost. But we wouldn’t count on seeing too many at your local track day.

It has been revealed that A lot has changed since Henry Ford won his first race; horsepower figures, aerodynamics, and suspension technology have come a long way. But the desire of the organization that bears his name to prove itself on the racetrack apparently hasn't changed much at all, and that’s something we’re certainly thankful for.

The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America.
  • Most people today haven’t heard of it.
  • Industry observers note that that loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America. The wooden steamship helped connect San Francisco with Fresh York City before the construction of a coast-to-coast rail network, and sank off the coast of South Carolina in 1857.

425 people died. Most people today haven’t heard of it.

Industry observers note that that loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship. But the SS Central America was also hauling $1.2 million worth of gold, according to a 1992 court case about the wreck. Given the current value of gold, that’s around $236 million in today’s dollars. And that’s just what’s documented: the ship had a number of wealthy passengers, who were likely carrying their own gold, so the total could be even higher.

A ship full of gold, sunk and lost for over a century. It’s odd that the ship isn’t a household name. And the story keeps getting weirder: the wreck contributed to a massive recession, and when treasure hunters found the ship in the 1980s, decades of lawsuits followed.

Sources indicate that say you wanted to get from San Francisco to Upcoming York City in the 1850s. Going over land was miserable—cars were a half century away, and there weren’t many roads. There wasn’t even a rail line connecting the two coasts. Your best bet was to take a ship down to what is now Panama, a train across that narrow bit of land, and then another ship up to New York.

The SS Central America served the Atlantic part of that journey. It left the east coast of Panama on September 3, 1857, with 592 people on board. The ship had one other stop: Havana, Cuba. By September 8, when the ship was leaving that port, the weather looked great, according to a writeup by the US Naval Institute.

Sources indicate that that changed—hurricane-force winds battered the wooden hull. By September 11, the crew was working to bail out the ship, and by noon every man joined them. It wasn’t enough: by 2pm the water reached the boilers, leaving the ship drifting. The bailing continued all night, and for a while it seemed like the weather would clear up long enough for a full evacuation. It wasn’t to be—the storm resumed by mid-morning. The captain signaled a nearby ship, the Marine, for help. Only 100 people—including the 59 women and children—boarded the Marine.

In a recent development, the captain went down with the ship around 8pm local time, along with most of the remaining men, who were pulled in by the undertow of the sinking ship. The few men who survived did so by grabbing doors, chairs, and anything else still floating, until another ship—the Ellen—could find them. In total, 425 people lost their lives.

The human cost was high, but there was also a huge economic fallout. A 1992 paper by Lawrence D. Stone, the researcher whose work led to the rediscovery of the wreck, states that the gold on board was intended to shore up several banks already on the brink of collapse. Within a month, almost all banks in the US stopped offering gold in exchange for paper money.

It has been revealed that naturally, a ship this famous—with this much gold on board—became a bit of a legend. Countless people attempted to find the wreck, but no one succeeded until the Columbus-America Discovery Group of Ohio found the wreck in the 1980s. The crew was led by treasure hunter Tommy Gregory Thompson.

In a recent development, the discovery happened thanks to advanced technology—sonar and state-of-the-art remote-controlled submarines. But also because of math.

Sources indicate that stone, whose work I mentioned earlier, explained his method in a 1992 paper. He employed Bayesian search theory. This method begins with finding hypotheses about where the wreck may be, judging how likely each theory is, and ultimately making a map outlining the probability of the ship being in various areas. A route for the search is designed to start with the highest probability areas, continuing from there to lower probabilities.

Industry observers note that the survey took 40 days, covering 1,400 square miles of ocean off the Carolina coast. The wreck ended up being in a relatively low probability area, though one included in the route. In 1988, a remotely operated vehicle provided a view of the wreck.

“The storybook result would have been for the Central America to have been found in a high probability area near the beginning of the search,” wrote Stone. “Given the actual result, what can we say about the value of the procedures for developing the search proposal? The most obvious thing to say is that they worked.”.

That’s the thing about probability: the most likely thing isn’t always what’s true. That doesn’t mean it’s not worth calculating—it can still lead to good results.

Industry observers note that but what about the gold? Over the next few years the team brought up most of the commercial gold shipment. A federal judge put its bullion value at about $21 million in 1993, but coins and ingots from a famous shipwreck are worth far more to collectors. In 2000, the bulk of it sold for about $50 million. Today most of the gold is in the hands of private collectors.

This would normally be where the story ends: the treasure is found, the treasure hunters get paid, and everyone is happy. That’s not what happened this time.

Industry observers note that by 1989, the insurance companies that covered the SS Central America back in the 1850s argued that the gold belonged to them. Their logic: We paid damages to clients who lost the gold, therefore it’s ours. The insurance companies lost that lawsuit, but it was only the beginning.

Sources indicate that thompson took $12.5 million from investors to fund the treasure hunt. Those investors sued in 2005, alleging they never got any proceeds from the treasure, even after the 2000 sale of the gold. Several members of Thompson’s crew sued in 2006. Thompson went into hiding in 2012, only to be arrested in 2015. He wasn’t released until March of 2026. Some 500 gold coins remain unaccounted for.

It’s an odd footnote to a fascinating story of history, math, and science. And who knows? Maybe this story will still be going a hundred years in the future.

And there may be more to the story of the SS Central America. A 2018 expedition recovered more gold from a safe on the ship, in a passenger compartment. There could be more down there.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie declared the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” indicates Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”.

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

Recent findings suggest that “Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”.

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company notes the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

#41164. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1289 w)

This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research demonstrates that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and revealed similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research demonstrates that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and revealed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

Sources indicate that it included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

Industry observers note that to measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

In a recent development, for free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

In a recent development, from this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

According to recent reports, the average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

In a recent development, the study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, mentioned that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, mentioned that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

According to recent reports, “It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she noted. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” stated Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she stated.

In a recent development, theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he remarked.

Sources indicate that “And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he remarked. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

Industry observers note that “I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

‘I Started Strength Training at 74. At 78, I Can Deadlift 132 Lbs—Here’s How.’

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing.
  • I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier.
  • After a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing. For most of my life, I’d been recreationally active, and had loved kayaking, swimming, and taking my dog on long walks. I’d never done any kind of structured strength training, until right before my 75th birthday. One day, I was sitting on a curb outside my house, and when it was time to stand up, I couldn’t. I felt embarrassed, and the idea of falling and not being able to get up or being in a situation where I couldn’t take care of myself was scary.

I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier. I also wanted to trust my body more, and feel confident in my ability to handle whatever life threw my way. So, I joined Aspire Athletic Club, a gym near my home in Schenectady, Newly introduced York, and began working out once a week with the owner, Chris Wertman. In the beginning, even simple movements were challenging, so I started with basic bodyweight exercises like the box squat, step-up, and bird dog. The focus was on learning proper form and getting comfortable with the movements.

After a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence. It was so encouraging to see the hard work pay off, and it motivated me to keep going. About a year into consistent training, I was feeling stronger and ready to take on more. I began training full-body twice a week and incorporated more challenging exercises like squat variations, the walking lunge, weighted glute bridge, and chest fly to build overall strength.

Industry observers note that I’d never deadlifted before, so seeing someone my age lift with that kind of strength was incredibly inspiring. That decision marked the beginning of a new chapter in my strength training journey—I told my new trainer of about six months, Jack Tyree, that I wanted to lift heavier weights and try deadlifting. I even began training for my gym’s upcoming annual deadlift exhibition, which was in eight months.

Since I’d just been training with dumbbells, I tried working with a kettlebell while I got comfortable with the movement and proper technique. As I got stronger and more confident, I graduated to the barbell and continued adding more weight each week. Then, this past May, I deadlifted 132 lbs for a single rep at the exhibition, setting a personal record. I never imagined I’d be able to do something like that, but I was so proud of how strong I’d become—and I was excited to see how much further I could push myself.

Industry observers note that six months after the exhibition, I now strength train three days a week: one day focused on upper body, one on lower body, and one dedicated to mobility and balance. Jack still programs all my workouts, and every session includes six to eight exercises, with 3 or 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps each. I use a mix of free weights and weight machines, and some of my go-to moves include the farmer’s carry, curtsy lunge, lat pulldown, scapular pushup, squat, and bench press. Deadlifts are still my favorite; I can now do three reps at 132 lbs, which I’m really proud of.

Industry observers note that outside the gym, I love getting outside and staying active, so I walk a few miles with my dog every day for my cardiovascular health. In addition to mobility and balance work at the gym, I also try to stretch at home whenever I can to ease muscle soreness and improve my range of motion, especially in my shoulders and hips.

I know nutrition is an important part of recovery too. Although I don’t follow a strict nutrition plan or count macros, I try to eat protein at every meal to support muscle growth. Usually, it’s chicken, red meat, or a scoop of protein powder mixed into my morning oatmeal. I also prioritize whole foods and aim to incorporate a variety of fruits and vegetables throughout the day.

Recent findings suggest that when I first started strength training, I didn’t know where to begin. So, having someone guide me through the movements, teach me proper form, and help me build strength safely made all the difference. My trainers have helped me recognize what I’m capable of, push beyond what I thought was possible, and progress at a pace that feels right. They also create workouts that challenge me while keeping my goals in mind. Having their support and encouragement has given me the confidence to try things I never imagined I could do. Whether it’s deadlifting heavy weights, bench pressing a barbell, or taking less rest between working sets, my trainers have taught me not to put a ceiling on what I think I can accomplish.

According to recent reports, before I strength trained, I felt weak and unsteady, but I didn’t give up and accept that I’d feel like that for the rest of my life. In some ways, I completely started over with exercise at 74 because I tried something brand new—and that’s affected my life outside of the gym.

Recent findings suggest that now, at 78, I feel stronger than ever; I can get up off the floor with ease, carry my own groceries into the house, shovel snow, garden, and play sports with my grandchildren. These are things I want to keep doing independently, and having the strength to do them confidently means the world to me. While I love lifting weights and hitting new PRs, the greatest reward is how much easier everyday life has become.

Learning to lift in my mid-70s wasn’t easy, and building that strength didn’t happen overnight, but I kept showing up, putting in the work, and gradually accomplishing what I once never thought was possible. Now, as I approach 80, I’m still getting stronger, and I want other women to know they’re never too old to get started, and they may be capable of far more than they realize. If I can go from struggling to get up from a curb to deadlifting 132 pounds, who knows what else is possible?

Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?
